## Regression Line

Last time, we saw that we can help summarize a scatterplot with a regression line

```{r}

library(haven)

dat <- read_dta("../../Data/Pleskac data.dta")

dat <- dat %>% filter(!is.na(polydrug) & !is.na(testeddrugs))

ggplot(dat, aes(KC, polydrug)) + geom_point() + stat_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_light()

```


## What is It?

- Best fitting "straight" line
- What is a line?
    - [Has slope and intercept]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
      - [$y = mx + b]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [**Intercept:** Value of $y$ when $x = 0$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [**Slope:** For one unit increase in $x$, how many units increase in $y$?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [How do we find this line?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    - [What does "best fitting" mean?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    


## Regression Vocabulary

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| message: false
#| fig.width: 5

set.seed(294)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- 9.94 + 4.81 * x + rnorm(100, sd = 3)

ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme_classic() +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
ggtitle("Correlation = .79, Intercept = 9.75, Slope = 4.51")
```
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}
1. **Criterion**: The variable we are trying to predict, which is on the $y$-axis (usually the DV)
2. **Predictor**: The variable used to predict the criterion, which is on the $x$-axis (usually the IV)
3. **Slope**: The steepness of the line
4. **Intercept**: The predicted value of the criterion when the predictor is at 0
:::

:::


## Regression Equation

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

The form of the simple linear regression model is as follows:

| Population | Sample |
| :--- | :--- |
| $y_{i} \mid x_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1}x_{i} + e_{i}$ | $y_{i} \mid x_{i} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1}x_{i} + e_{i}$ |
| $\hat{y}_{i} = b_{0} + b_{1}x_{i}$ | $\hat{y}_{i} = \hat{b}_{0} + \hat{b}_{1}x_{i}$ |

1. $y_i \mid x_i$: The **conditional** mean value of $y_i$ given a fixed/specific value of $x_i$
2. $\hat{y}_i$: Estimated outcome ($\hat{\,\,\,}$: an estimated value)
3. $b_0$ ($\hat{b}_0$): The (estimated) intercept (predicted value of $y_i$ when $x_i = 0$)
4. $b_1$ ($\hat{b}_1$): The (estimated) slope (predicted increase in $y_i$ for a one-unit increase in $x_i$)
5. $e_i = y - \hat{y}$:
    + The **residual** or **error** when predicting $y_i$ from $x_i$
    + The **difference** between a particular point and the regression line
    
::: 

```{r}
#| include: false

set.seed(294)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- 9.94 + 4.81 * x + rnorm(100, sd = 3)

# Base plots
png("Regression1.png", width = 960, height = 960, res = 200)
ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green)
dev.off()

png("Regression2.png", width = 960, height = 960, res = 200)
ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
  geom_point(aes(0, 9.75), col = my_blue, size = I(4))
dev.off()

# Plot 3 with '1 unit x' label and slope 'b' annotation
png("Regression3.png", width = 960, height = 960, res = 200)
ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
  geom_point(aes(0, 9.75), col = my_blue, size = I(4)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 2, y = 14.26, yend = 14.26), col = my_red, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.02, "npc"))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2, xend = 2, y = 14.26, yend = 18.77), col = my_red, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.02, "npc"))) +
  # White background box for "1 unit x"
  annotate("label", x = 1.5, y = 13.3, label = "bold('1 unit ') ~ italic(x)", parse = TRUE, color = my_red, fill = "white", label.size = NA, size = 4.5) +
  # Slope label b
  annotate("text", x = 2.15, y = 16.5, label = "italic(b)", parse = TRUE, color = my_red, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold")
dev.off()

# Plot 4 with slope annotations plus residual 'e_i' annotation
png("Regression4.png", width = 960, height = 960, res = 200)
ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) + geom_point() + theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
  geom_point(aes(0, 9.75), col = my_blue, size = I(4)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 2, y = 14.26, yend = 14.26), col = my_red, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.02, "npc"))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 2, xend = 2, y = 14.26, yend = 18.77), col = my_red, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.02, "npc"))) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = -2.212038, xend = -2.212038, y = -.2262914, yend = -4.979711), col = my_purple) +
  geom_point(aes(-2.212038, -4.979711), col = my_purple, size = I(3)) +
  # White background box for "1 unit x"
  annotate("label", x = 1.5, y = 13.3, label = "bold('1 unit ') ~ italic(x)", parse = TRUE, color = my_red, fill = "white", label.size = NA, size = 4.5) +
  # Slope label b
  annotate("text", x = 2.15, y = 16.5, label = "italic(b)", parse = TRUE, color = my_red, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold") +
  # Residual label e_i
  annotate("text", x = -1.85, y = -3.5, label = "italic(e)[i]", parse = TRUE, color = my_purple, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold")
dev.off()

# Plot 5 with constant normal distributions + clean, non-overlapping annotations at x = 0.5
fit <- lm(y ~ x)
sigma_val <- summary(fit)$sigma
x_centers <- c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)

# Calculate normal density curves at each x position
dist_df <- map_dfr(x_centers, function(x0) {
  y0 <- predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(x = x0))
  y_seq <- seq(y0 - 3 * sigma_val, y0 + 3 * sigma_val, length.out = 100)
  dens <- dnorm(y_seq, mean = y0, sd = sigma_val)
  scale_factor <- 3.5 
  tibble(
    x0 = x0,
    y0 = y0,
    y = y_seq,
    x_curve = x0 + dens * scale_factor
  )
})

dist_summary <- dist_df %>%
  group_by(x0) %>%
  summarise(
    y0 = first(y0),
    y_min = min(y),
    y_max = max(y),
    x_peak = max(x_curve),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Target point for numerical coordinate annotation (at x = 0.5)
coord_target <- dist_summary %>% filter(x0 == 0.5)

png("Regression5.png", width = 960, height = 960, res = 200)
ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
  # Vertical dotted axis for each distribution
  geom_segment(data = dist_summary, aes(x = x0, xend = x0, y = y_min, yend = y_max), 
               col = my_blue, linetype = "dotted", size = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Horizontal dotted peak indicator
  geom_segment(data = dist_summary, aes(x = x0, xend = x_peak, y = y0, yend = y0), 
               col = my_blue, linetype = "dotted", size = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Normal density curve
  geom_path(data = dist_df, aes(x = x_curve, y = y, group = x0), 
            col = my_blue, size = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Red square box with cross at predicted mean
  geom_point(data = dist_summary, aes(x = x0, y = y0), 
             shape = 7, col = my_red, size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Numerical coordinate annotation label (nudged up and left off the line)
  geom_label(data = coord_target, 
             aes(x = x0, y = y0, 
                 label = paste0("(", sprintf("%.2f", x0), ", ", sprintf("%.2f", y0), ")")), 
             nudge_x = -0.45, nudge_y = 2.0, col = my_red, fill = "white", 
             fontface = "bold", size = 4.2, label.size = NA, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Arrow pointing to the x = 0.5 curve from high above the regression line
  annotate("segment", x = 1.25, xend = 0.88, y = 18.5, yend = 15.2,
           col = my_purple, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.02, "npc")), size = 0.9) +
  # Text label sigma_epsilon
  annotate("text", x = 1.30, y = 19.2, label = "s[epsilon]", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_purple, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold")
dev.off()



# Plot 6: Univariate distribution of y ignoring x (oriented vertically)
mean_y <- mean(y)
sd_y <- sd(y)

# Calculate overall vertical density curve for y
y_seq_total <- seq(mean_y - 3 * sd_y, mean_y + 3 * sd_y, length.out = 100)
dens_total <- dnorm(y_seq_total, mean = mean_y, sd = sd_y)
scale_factor_total <- 4.5

total_dist_df <- tibble(
  y = y_seq_total,
  x_curve = dens_total * scale_factor_total
)

png("Regression6.png", width = 960, height = 960, res = 200)
ggplot() +
  # Univariate y data points plotted along x = 0
  geom_point(data = tibble(x = 0, y = y), aes(x = x, y = y), alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_classic() +
  # Vertical dotted center line
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 0, y = min(y_seq_total), yend = max(y_seq_total)), 
               col = my_blue, linetype = "dotted", size = 0.8) +
  # Horizontal dashed line at overall mean y (y-bar)
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_y, col = my_red, linetype = "dashed", size = 0.8) +
  # Vertical normal density curve
  geom_path(data = total_dist_df, aes(x = x_curve, y = y), 
            col = my_blue, size = 1) +
  # Highlighted point/marker at overall mean y
  geom_point(aes(x = 0, y = mean_y), shape = 7, col = my_red, size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2) +
  # Annotation for y-bar (overall mean)
  annotate("text", x = -0.12, y = mean_y, label = "bar(y)", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_red, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1) +
  # Arrow pointing to the curve for s_y (total standard deviation of y)
  annotate("segment", x = 0.60, xend = max(total_dist_df$x_curve) * 0.85, 
           y = mean_y + sd_y + 1.5, yend = mean_y + sd_y,
           col = my_purple, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.02, "npc")), size = 0.9) +
  # Annotation for s_y
  annotate("text", x = 0.65, y = mean_y + sd_y + 2.2, label = "s[y]", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_purple, size = 5.5, fontface = "bold") +
  # Match y-limits to previous regression plots for side-by-side visual comparison
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-5, 22)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.8, 1.2), breaks = NULL, name = "") +
  labs(y = "y")
dev.off()
```

- [**(0.50, 12.00)**]{style="color: #E41A1C;"} is a point on the best fit line
- For all cases where $x = 0.50$, our estimated mean of $\bar{y} | (x = 0.50) = 12.00$ 
    - The standard deviation of $y$ when $x = 0.50$ is $s_y | (x = 0.50) = \color{#984EA3} s_{\epsilon} = 3.27$
      - In fact, this what we are saying the SD of $y$ is for **any** value of $x$, $\sy |x= \color{#984EA3} s_{\epsilon} = 3.27$ 
- For any given $x$, the regression line tells us the expected mean of $y$, with constant SD

:::

:::

## Normal Equations

The best-fit line follows the form:

$$\hat{y}_i = \hat{b}_0 + \hat{b}_1 x_i$$

The estimated regression coefficients ($\hat{b}_0$ and $\hat{b}_1$) are functions of familiar descriptive statistics:

$$\hat{b}_1 = \frac{s_{xy}}{s^2_{x}}$$

$$\hat{b}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{b}_1 \bar{x}$$

These are known as the **normal equations**


## Ordinary Least Squares


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Where do these "normal equations" come from?

Method of **ordinary least squares** (OLS):

- Find $b_0$ and $b_1$ that minimize the sum of squared differences between $y_i$ and $\hat{y}$
- In symbols:

$$(\hat{b}_0, \hat{b}_1)^\prime  = \underset{b_{0},b_{1}}{\text{argmin}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\right] \\
   = \underset{b_{0},b_{1}}{\text{argmin}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^N(y_i - b_0 - b_1x_i)^2\right]$$

OLS is the same **loss function** we use in ANOVA: minimize (sums of) squared errors between $\hat{y}_i$'s and the observed $y_i$'s


:::



## Standard Error of the Estimate

$$s_{y\cdot x} =\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}{N-2}} = \sqrt{\frac{SS_{\text{residual}}}{df}}$$

- $s_{y \cdot x}$ is the standard deviation of $y$ predicted from $x$
    - Notice the "$\cdot$" between $y$ and $x$
- $s_{y \cdot x}^2$ is an unbiased estimator of $\sigma_{y \cdot x}^2$
- $s^2_{y\cdot x}$ is a measure of the accuracy of the regression line
- $s_{y\cdot x}$ is in the units of $y$



## R-Squared

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

$R^2 = r_{xy}^2$ is the effect size of the simple linear regression model

- Proportion of the variance of $y$ accounted for by $x$


Sample variation of $\color{#FF7F00}{\underset{\text{\small sum of\\squares}}{{SS_y}}}$ = numerator of sample variance of y


$$SS_y = \sum_{i=1}^N(y_i - \bar{y})^2$$

$(y_i - \bar{y})$ can be decomposed into two parts:

$$
\color{#377EB8}{\underbrace{\color{black}{(y_i - \bar{y})}}_{\substack{\nearrow \\[0.2em] \text{\textbf{total}} \\ \text{variation of } y}}}
= 
\color{#984EA3}{\underbrace{\color{black}{(y_i - \hat{y}_i)}}_{\substack{\uparrow \\[0.2em] \text{variation of } y \\ \text{\textbf{NOT} predicted by } x}}} 
+ 
\color{#4DAF4A}{\underbrace{\color{black}{(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})}}_{\substack{\nwarrow \\[0.2em] \text{variation of } y \\ \text{predicted by } x}}}
$$

:::


## R-Squared

Sample variation of $y$ ($SS_y$) can be decomposed into two parts:

$$SS_y = SS_{\text{residual}} + SS_{\text{regression}} \\
  \sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2  = \sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \sum(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2$$

- $SS_{\text{residual}}$: variation of the residuals
  - Like $SS_{\text{within}}$ from ANOVA

- $SS_{\text{regression}}$: variation of $y$ predicted by $x$
  - Like $SS_{\text{between}}$ from ANOVA

$$R^2 = \frac{SS_{\text{regression}}}{SS_y} = 1 - \frac{SS_{\text{residual}}}{SS_y}$$

In the simple regression model, $R^2 = r^2_{xy}$

- Proportion of variation in $y$ accounted for by $\hat{y}$

## R-Squared Viz 1


```{r}
#| message: false

set.seed(294)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- 9.94 + 4.81 * x + rnorm(100, sd = 3)



ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_light() +
  
  # Lines
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_orange, size = I(1.5)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(y), col = my_red, size = I(1.5)) +
  
  # ARROWS (Corrected Color Alignment)
  # 1. Residual (y_i - y_hat): point to regression line -> PURPLE
  geom_segment(aes(x = x[70], y = y[70], xend = x[70], yend = predict(lm(y ~ x))[70]),
               col = my_purple, arrow = arrow(length = unit(.1, "inches"), ends = "both"), size = 0.8) +
  # 2. Total Variation (y_i - y_bar): point to mean line -> BLUE
  geom_segment(aes(x = x[57], y = y[57], xend = x[57], yend = mean(y)),
               col = my_blue, arrow = arrow(length = unit(.1, "inches"), ends = "both"), size = 0.8) +
  # 3. Regression Variation (y_hat - y_bar): mean line to regression line -> GREEN
  geom_segment(aes(x = .9, y = mean(y), xend = .9, yend = predict(lm(y ~ x), newdata = data.frame(x = .9))),
               col = my_green, arrow = arrow(length = unit(.1, "inches"), ends = "both"), size = 0.8) +

  # LINE LABELS
  annotate("text", x = -2.2, y = mean(y) + 2.0, label = "bar(y)", parse = TRUE, col = my_red, size = 6, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.2, y = 1.0, label = "hat(y)", parse = TRUE, col = my_orange, size = 6, fontface = "bold") +

  # BOX 1: SS_reg (Top Left - Green)
  annotate("label", x = -2.1, y = 16.5, 
           label = "atop(SS[reg] == SS(hat(y)[i] - bar(y)), atop(bold('Variation in ') ~ italic(y), bold('predicted by ') ~ italic(x)))", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_green, fill = "white", label.size = 0.8, size = 4.2) +
  
  # BOX 2: SS_resid (Middle Right - Purple)
  annotate("label", x = 1.3, y = 6.5, 
           label = "atop(SS[resid] == SS(y[i] - hat(y)[i]), atop(bold('Variation in ') ~ italic(y) ~ bold('NOT'), bold('predicted by ') ~ italic(x)))", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_purple, fill = "white", label.size = 0.8, size = 4.2) +

  # BOX 3: SS_y (Bottom Right - Blue)
  annotate("label", x = 0.6, y = -3.0, 
           label = "atop(SS[y] == SS(y[i] - bar(y)), bold('Variation in ') ~ italic(y))", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_blue, fill = "white", label.size = 0.8, size = 4.2) +

  # R^2 COLORED FRACTION FORMULA (Fixed parse syntax for R^2 =)
  annotate("text", x = 1.40, y = -3.2, label = "R^2 ~ '='", parse = TRUE, col = "black", size = 6.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1.65, xend = 2.05, y = -3.2, yend = -3.2, col = "black", size = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.85, y = -2.3, label = "SS[reg]", parse = TRUE, col = my_green, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.85, y = -4.1, label = "SS[y]", parse = TRUE, col = my_blue, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold")
```

$R^2$ represents how **different** the best fitting regression line is along the $y$-axis than the simple mean of $y$


## R-Squared Viz 2

```{r}
#| message: false

set.seed(294)
x <- rnorm(100)
y <- 9.94 + 4.81 * x + rnorm(100, sd = 3)



ggplot(tibble(x, y), aes(x, y)) +

  # Lines

  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(y), col = my_red, size = I(1.5)) +

  # 1. Residual (y_i - y_hat): point to regression line -> PURPLE
  geom_segment(aes(x = x[70], y = y[70], xend = x[70], yend = predict(lm(y ~ x))[70]),

  # 2. Total Variation (y_i - y_bar): point to mean line -> BLUE
  geom_segment(aes(x = x[57], y = y[57], xend = x[57], yend = mean(y)),

  # 3. Regression Variation (y_hat - y_bar): mean line to regression line -> GREEN

  # LINE LABELS

  annotate("text", x = -2.2, y = 1.0, label = "hat(y)", parse = TRUE, col = my_orange, size = 6, fontface = "bold") +

  # BOX 1: SS_reg (Top Left - Green)
  annotate("label", x = -2.1, y = 16.5, 
           label = "atop(SS[reg] == SS(hat(y)[i] - bar(y)), atop(bold('Variation in ') ~ italic(y), bold('predicted by ') ~ italic(x)))", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_green, fill = "white", label.size = 0.8, size = 4.2) +
  
  # BOX 2: SS_resid (Middle Right - Purple)
  annotate("label", x = 1.3, y = 6.5, 
           label = "atop(SS[resid] == SS(y[i] - hat(y)[i]), atop(bold('Variation in ') ~ italic(y) ~ bold('NOT'), bold('predicted by ') ~ italic(x)))", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_purple, fill = "white", label.size = 0.8, size = 4.2) +

  # BOX 3: SS_y (Bottom Center-Left - Blue, shifted left to x = 0.15)
  annotate("label", x = 0.15, y = -3.0, 
           label = "atop(SS[y] == SS(y[i] - bar(y)), bold('Variation in ') ~ italic(y))", 
           parse = TRUE, col = my_blue, fill = "white", label.size = 0.8, size = 4.2) +

  # R^2 ALTERNATIVE FORMULA: R^2 = 1 - SS_resid / SS_y
  annotate("text", x = 1.25, y = -3.2, label = "R^2 ~ '= 1 -'", parse = TRUE, col = "black", size = 6.5) +
  annotate("segment", x = 1.58, xend = 2.05, y = -3.2, yend = -3.2, col = "black", size = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.81, y = -2.3, label = "SS[resid]", parse = TRUE, col = my_purple, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.81, y = -4.1, label = "SS[y]", parse = TRUE, col = my_blue, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold")
```

$R^2$ represents how much **smaller** the residuals are for the regression line than for the simple mean of $y$

## Adjusted R-Squared

- $R^2$ is a positively biased estimate of the population squared correlation
- Adjusted $R^2$ is less biased, but not completely unbiased
- For simple linear regression:

$$\text{Adjusted }R^2 = \left(R^2 - \frac{1}{N-1}\right)\left(\frac{N-1}{N-2}\right)$$

## Standardized Regression

What happens if we standardize $x$ and $y$?

What is standardization?

- [Converts a variable to $Z$-score units]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [$Z_x = \frac{x -\bar{x}}{s_x}$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [$Z_y = \frac{y -\bar{y}}{s_y}$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [**New Intercept Interpretation:** $Z_y$ when $Z_x = 0$ (Always 0)]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [**New Slope Interpretation:** Increase in $Z_y$ for one unit increase in $Z_x$ ($r_{xy}$)]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
    
    
    

## Map to Correlation

**Standardized regression coefficients** are those that describe the relationship between standardized variables

Standardized $\hat{b}_0 = 0$ and $\hat{b}_1 = r_{xy}$.

Unstandardized $\hat{b}_1 = \frac{r_{xy}s_y}{s_x}$

Unstandardized $\hat{b}_0 = \bar{y} - \hat{b}_1\bar{x}$ (unstandardized $\hat{b}_1$)


## Test for Intercept


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}


- $H_0: b_0 = 0$
- $H_1: b_0 \neq 0$
- $b_0$ is population regression intercept (sample statistic = $\hat{b}_0$)

$$t_{\text{obs}}(df) = \frac{\hat{b}_0}{s_{\hat{b}_0}} \hspace{1cm}   s_{\hat{b}_0}= \sqrt{\left(\frac{(1 - r^2_{xy})\times\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2}{df}\right)\left(\frac{1}{N} + \frac{\bar{x}^2}{(N-1)\times s^2_{x}}\right)}$$

:::

## Intercept Test Terms

- $df$: degrees of freedom = $N - 2$
- $s_x^2$: sample variance of $x$
- $\bar{y}$: sample mean of $y$
- $\bar{x}$: sample mean of $x$
- $r_{xy}$: sample correlation between $x$ and $y$

Under $H_0$, $t_{\text{obs}}(df)$ is $t$-distributed with $df = N - 2$ degrees of freedom

Confidence interval:

$$\hat{b}_0 \pm t(df)_{\alpha/2} \times s_{\hat{b}_0}$$

## Why Care?

What is the interpretation of the intercept?


- [Estimated mean of $y$ when $x = 0$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [Test is whether $\bar{y}|(x=0) \neq 0$ when $x = 0$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [Is 0 a plausible value for $x$?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [Is 0 a plausible value for $y$?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- [Do you care specifically about $\bar{y}|(x=0)$?]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}



## Test for Slope

* $H_0: b_1 = 0$
* $H_1: b_1 \neq 0$
* $b_1$ is population regression slope of $x$ on $y$ (sample statistic = $\hat{b}_1$)

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
$$t_{\text{obs}}(df) = \frac{\hat{b}_1}{s_{\hat{b}_1}}$$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
$$s_{\hat{b}_1}= \frac{s_y}{s_x}\sqrt{\frac{1 - r^2_{xy}}{df}}$$
:::

:::

## Slope Test Terms

* $df$: degrees of freedom = $N - 2$
* $s_y$: sample $SD$ of $y$
* $s_x$: sample $SD$ of $x$
* $r_{xy}$: sample correlation between $x$ and $y$

Under $H_0$, $t_{\text{obs}}(df)$ is $t$-distributed with $df = N - 2$ degrees of freedom

Confidence interval:

$$\hat{b}_1 \pm t(df)_{\alpha/2} \times s_{\hat{b}_1}$$


## Hypothesis Tests for $R^2$


* $H_0$: population $R^2 = 0$
* $H_1$: population $R^2 > 0$ (note: $R^2$ cannot be negative)

$$F_{\text{obs}}(1, N-2) = \frac{MS_{\text{regression}}}{MS_{\text{residual}}}$$

* $MS_{\text{regression}} = \frac{SS_{\text{regression}}}{1}$ ($MS$: "mean squares")
* $MS_{\text{residual}} = \frac{SS_{\text{residual}}}{N-2}$
* $N$: sample size

Under $H_0$, $F_{\text{obs}}$ follows the $F$ distribution with 1 and $N-2$ $df$

## Test Equivalence

For **simple** regression (just one $x$), the following tests are all equivalent:

- $t$-test of correlation $r_{xy}$
- $t$-test of regression slope $b_1$
- $F$-test of $R^2$

## Why $N-2$ $df$?

- How many (which) parameters are we estimating in a simple regression?
  - [One intercept and one slope. That's why we "lose" 2 $df$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}



## Assumptions

1. All observations are **conditionally** independent
  - Nothing about one observation of $x$ tells you anything about any other observation of $x$ that $y$ doesn't already tell you (and vice versa)
2. No outliers
3. Across each predictor value, **residuals** are normally distributed with mean 0 and constant variance (homoscedasticity)
    - Equivalently put: There is a linear relationship between $x$ and $y$
    - New version of the normality and homogeneity of variance assumptions




## Residual Assumptions

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="60%"}
![](Regression5)
:::

::: {.column width="40%"}






- For every point on the $x$ axis
    - Residuals follow a normal distribution
    - Variance (SD) of $y$ is constant



:::

:::


## Non-Normal Residuals


```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

set.seed(294)
n <- 400
x_nonnormal <- rnorm(n)
shape_p <- 2.0
scale_p <- 2.5

# Right-skewed gamma residuals centered at zero
e_skew <- rgamma(n, shape = shape_p, scale = scale_p) - (shape_p * scale_p)
y_nonnormal <- 9.94 + 4.81 * x_nonnormal + e_skew

fit_nonnormal <- lm(y_nonnormal ~ x_nonnormal)
x_centers <- c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)

# Calculate right-skewed conditional density curves
dist_df_nonnormal <- map_dfr(x_centers, function(x0) {
  y0 <- predict(fit_nonnormal, newdata = data.frame(x_nonnormal = x0))
  g_seq <- seq(0.01, 16, length.out = 100)
  dens <- dgamma(g_seq, shape = shape_p, scale = scale_p)
  y_vals <- y0 - (shape_p * scale_p) + g_seq
  scale_factor <- 8.0
  tibble(
    x0 = x0,
    y0 = y0,
    y = y_vals,
    x_curve = x0 + dens * scale_factor
  )
})

dist_summary_nonnormal <- dist_df_nonnormal %>%
  group_by(x0) %>%
  summarise(
    y0 = first(y0),
    y_min = min(y),
    y_max = max(y),
    x_peak = max(x_curve),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(tibble(x = x_nonnormal, y = y_nonnormal), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
  # Vertical dotted center axis
  geom_segment(data = dist_summary_nonnormal, aes(x = x0, xend = x0, y = y_min, yend = y_max), 
               col = my_blue, linetype = "dotted", size = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Asymmetric, right-skewed density curves
  geom_path(data = dist_df_nonnormal, aes(x = x_curve, y = y, group = x0), 
            col = my_blue, size = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Predicted mean marker
  geom_point(data = dist_summary_nonnormal, aes(x = x0, y = y0), 
             shape = 7, col = my_red, size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE)

```


## Heteroscedasticity

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 6

set.seed(6543)
n <- 400
x_het <- rnorm(n)

# Residual standard deviation increases linearly with x
sd_het <- 0.8 + 4.0 * (x_het - min(x_het)) / (max(x_het) - min(x_het))
y_het <- 9.94 + 4.81 * x_het + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sd_het)

fit_het <- lm(y_het ~ x_het)
x_centers <- c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)

# Calculate conditional normal density curves with expanding variance
dist_df_het <- map_dfr(x_centers, function(x0) {
  y0 <- predict(fit_het, newdata = data.frame(x_het = x0))
  sigma_x0 <- 0.8 + 4.0 * (x0 - min(x_het)) / (max(x_het) - min(x_het))
  y_seq <- seq(y0 - 3 * sigma_x0, y0 + 3 * sigma_x0, length.out = 100)
  dens <- dnorm(y_seq, mean = y0, sd = sigma_x0)
  scale_factor <- 8.0 
  tibble(
    x0 = x0,
    y0 = y0,
    y = y_seq,
    x_curve = x0 + dens * scale_factor
  )
})

dist_summary_het <- dist_df_het %>%
  group_by(x0) %>%
  summarise(
    y0 = first(y0),
    y_min = min(y),
    y_max = max(y),
    x_peak = max(x_curve),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(tibble(x = x_het, y = y_het), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, col = my_green) +
  # Vertical dotted center axis
  geom_segment(data = dist_summary_het, aes(x = x0, xend = x0, y = y_min, yend = y_max), 
               col = my_blue, linetype = "dotted", size = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Horizontal dotted peak indicator
  geom_segment(data = dist_summary_het, aes(x = x0, xend = x_peak, y = y0, yend = y0), 
               col = my_blue, linetype = "dotted", size = 0.8, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Density curves showing expanding spread
  geom_path(data = dist_df_het, aes(x = x_curve, y = y, group = x0), 
            col = my_blue, size = 0.9, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  # Predicted mean marker
  geom_point(data = dist_summary_het, aes(x = x0, y = y0), 
             shape = 7, col = my_red, size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE)

```




## Role of Assumptions


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

Models can be used for different purposes:

- Describe
- Predict
- Decide

Our assumptions are **primarily** used to delineate the conditions under which hypothesis tests have known properties. 

- e.g., $\alpha$ equals true Type I error rate

However they also can set the terms for which are descriptions can be correct and our predictions are likely to be accurate. 

- There are techniques to improve predictions under assumption violations (beyond this course)

:::




## Example

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}

**Original Study**:

Pleskac, T. J. (2008). Decision making and learning while taking sequential risks. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*, *34*, 167-185.

**Replication study link**: [https://osf.io/3amj4](https://osf.io/3amj4)

:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}


To what extent is the learning aspect of risk-taking behavior related to risky drug use?

ART = Angling Risk Tasks, computer game to study risk-taking behavior

Game play:

- Subjects decide whether to cast a rod to catch fish in a pond
- If red fish is caught, earn 5 cents and a chance to cast again
- If blue fish is caught, end the round & lose money
- Play 30 rounds per study condition
- Subjects were compensated based on their winnings

:::

## Details

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

**Conditions**:

- Weather:
    - Sunny day (S): subjects can see # of red & blue fish in the pond
    - Cloudy day (C): subjects cannot see # each type of fish
    - In cloudy day condition, subjects can learn about probabilities
- Type of fishing:
    - Catch n' release (R): probabilities of red and blue fish are constant
    - Catch n' keep (K): probabilities change with successive casts

Each subject was exposed to 30 reps of all 4 combinations of conditions:

- KS, KC, RS, RC

**Variables**:

- Polydrug: count of the number of risky/illegal drugs ever tried (11 categories), weighted by frequency of use
- ART scores (for each KS, KC, RS, RC): average number of casts taken on trials for which subjects chose to stop fishing (no blue fish)

:::

## More Details



Original comparisons of interest:

- Are the correlations between ART scores and polydrug in the sunny conditions greater than the correlations for the cloudy conditions?

Let's test a simpler hypothesis:

- Are KC scores related to real-life risk-taking behavior (polydrug)?
    - Catch n' keep on a cloudy day
    


## Example

```{r}
#| echo: true

lm1 <- lm(polydrug ~ KC, dat)
summary(lm1)
```
## Results

$$\widehat{\text{polydrug}} = \hat{b}_0 + \hat{b}_1 \text{KC}$$

| Coefficient | Estimate | SE | $t$ | $p$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Intercept ($\hat{b}_0$)** | 7.46 | 1.01 | 7.41 | <.001 |
| **KC ($\hat{b}_1$)** | -0.01 | 0.02 | -0.56 | .574 |

$R^2 = 0.002, F(1, 151) = 0.32, p = .57$
    
## Interpretations

- Intercept = 7.45 ($p < .001$)
    - [When KC = 0, the estimated mean of polydrug = 7.45, which is significantly different from the mean of polydrug being 0]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- Slope = -0.01 ($p = .57$)
    - [For one unit increase in KC, we expect a 0.01 unit decrease in polydrug, which is not significantly different from a 0 unit decrease]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
- $R^2 = 0.002$ ($p = .57$)
    - [KC explains 0.2% of the variance in polydrug, which is not significantly different from 0]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}


## Standardization

We can use the `scale()` function to standardize variables and then review the standardized regression result


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
dat <- dat |> 
  mutate(Z_KC = scale(KC),
         Z_polydrug = scale(polydrug))

std_lm1 <- lm(Z_polydrug ~ Z_KC, dat)
summary(std_lm1)
```

## Standardized Results

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
dat <- dat |> 
  mutate(Z_KC = scale(KC),
         Z_polydrug = scale(polydrug))

std_lm1 <- lm(Z_polydrug ~ Z_KC, dat)
summary(std_lm1)
```

## Map to Correlation

Note that in the standardized result:
- $b_0 \approx 0$ (slightly different due to rounding) 
- $b_1 = r_{\text{KC, polydrug}}$*

```{r}
#| echo: true

cor(dat$KC, dat$polydrug)
```

* Only for regression with a single predictor!
    
## Assumption Checks

Assumptions are typically check graphically

- **Normality:** QQ Plot of **residuals**
- **homoscedasticity:** 
    - Plot $x$ variable along $x$-axis
    - Plot residuals along $y$-axis
    - Spread of residuals (vertically) should be uniform for different values of $x$ variable (horizontal)
    
## QQ Residuals

First we use `residuals()` function to extract residuals

```{r}
#| echo: true
dat$residuals <- residuals(lm1)
```


Then we can create a QQ plot like we've learned

```{r}
#| fig.height: 4
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
ggplot(dat, aes(sample = residuals)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(col = my_red) +
  theme_light()
```

## QQ Plot

```{r}
#| fig.height: 4
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
ggplot(dat, aes(sample = residuals)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(col = my_red) +
theme_light()
```

## Homoscedasticity

For homoscedasticity, I will 

- Plot $x$-values along $x$-axis 
- Residuals along $y$-axis
- Add horizontal reference line at $y = 0$
- Points should be uniformly and noisily spread around reference line


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
ggplot(dat, aes(KC, residuals)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = my_blue) +
  geom_point() + theme_light()
```

## Homoscedasticity Plot

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
ggplot(dat, aes(KC, residuals)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = my_blue) +
  xlab("KC") + ylab("Residual") +
  geom_point() + theme_light()
```

## Interpretations

- Normality seems somewhat violated
  - Tails of QQ Plot deviate from reference line
  - If $N$ is large enough, relatively robust to violations of normality due to central limit theorem
- Homoscedasticity seems somewhat violated (aka relationship is heteroscedastic)
    - Variance seems a bit larger for small values of KC than large values of KC
    - Heteroscedasticity can bias standard errors of regression coefficients (more on this in multiple regression lectures)
    
## APA Writeup

A simple linear regression of Catch and Keep scores on a Cloudy Day (KC) on risk taking behavior was not significant, $F(1, 151) = 0.32, p = .56, R^2 = 0.002$. The intercept was significantly different from zero, $b_0 = 7.45, t(151) = 7.41, p < .001$. The slope was not significantly different from zero, $b_1 = -0.01, t(151) = 0.56, p = .57$

(I usually wouldn't include the intercept, but put it here for reference)

## Bayesian Version

We can do simple regression in `rstanarm` exactly as we have seen every other time we have estimated a linear model (it's more what `rstanarm` was built to do!)

- With a uniform prior, posterior mean of $b_0$ and $b_1$ will be identical to OLS solution
- Stronger priors might cause posterior means to differ

## Bayesian Example

```{r}
library(rstanarm)
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

stan_lm1 <- stan_glm(polydrug ~ KC, dat, 
                     family = "gaussian", 
                     seed = 12340)

summary(stan_lm1)
```

## Bayesian Output

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true


stan_lm1 <- stan_glm(polydrug ~ KC, dat, 
                     family = "gaussian", 
                     seed = 12340)

summary(stan_lm1, probs = c(.025, .5, .975), digits = 2)

```


## HDI Intervals

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
library(bayestestR)
hdi(stan_lm1, component = "all")
```
  
## Bayesian $R^2$ Review

::: {style="font-size: .9em;"}

Because Bayesian estimates aren't deterministic the way the simple OLS algorithm is, the traditional $R^2$ is not guaranteed to be $0 \leq R^2 \leq 1$

- Means it is possible for the model to explain more than the total variance
    - Not a sensible interpretation!
    
Alternative:

$$\text{Bayesian } R^2 = \frac{s_{\hat{y}}^2}{s_{\hat{y}}^2 + s_{\epsilon}^2}$$


- Is guaranteed to be $0 \leq \text{Bayesian } R^2 \leq 1$
- Same interpretation as $\eta^2$ and $R^2$

::: 



## Bayesian $R^2$

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
library(performance)
r2_bayes(stan_lm1)
```


## Bayesian APA Writeup

Using Bayesian estimation, we fit a simple regression of Catch and Keep scores on a Cloudy Day (KC) on risk taking behavior. The intercept had a posterior mean $b_0 = 7.46, 95% CI = [5.46, 9.39]$. The slope had a posterior mean $b_1 = -0.01, 95% CI = [-0.06, 0.03]$. The posterior mean Bayesian $R^2 = 0.004, 95% CI = [<.001, 0.031]$, suggesting KC scores explained between 0 and 3% of the variance in risk taking behavior. 

(I usually wouldn't include the intercept, but put it here for reference)
